terms.meaning: A program that applies written rules to an answer and says pass or fail for each rule. Because it only follows rules, it gives the same verdict every time.
Same input, same verdict, every time. The AI that writes an answer can vary from run to run. A checker that follows rules does not.
One thing a good answer must do.
The pass or fail rule for a criterion, written as a sentence, such as under 150 words.

The threshold needs human judgment, so a checker cannot decide it. That criterion is not covered until you rewrite the threshold as a number, a list of terms or a label. It stays visible as not covered and is left out of the score. This course never hands such a criterion to an AI grader.
A decision made when words were turned into a rule, such as whole word or part of a word. If it is not what you meant, change the sentence.
A made-up output used to test the checker itself, where you already know the right verdict. A useful pair is one clearly bad output and one that is polished but wrong.
An output that reads well but breaks a requirement. If your checker passes it, one of your checks is only for show, like window dressing.

In this course, a record of what each fixture was built to fail, judged against your requirements. It is written only after you lock your predictions, and you read it after the checker has run. The idea is that nothing can influence a prediction made before the result.
In this course, one answer from your prompt, produced in a new chat. A new chat means a new CLI process. The idea is that one run is one draw, so you collect several.
Your starting score: for each criterion, the pass rate across several answers, recorded once your thresholds are settled. A later change is compared against it. Part 4 tries to beat it.
A number a program returns when it finishes. 0 usually means everything went well, and a checker may use another number, such as 1, to say that something failed.
In this course, an open-source tool used on the promptfoo track. It does the same job as the checker script, using a config file. The idea is the same rules written in a different form.
In this course, a SKILL.md instruction file that your agent follows to do one job. The idea is a rulebook you can read and hold the agent to.
In this course, your Part 1 prompt, with your rough notes included. It is the exact text the AI receives on every run. The idea is that the prompt is the thing being measured.
In this course, your criteria and thresholds from Part 2. It is the spec for your checker. The idea is that the written rules come first and the checker follows them.
In this course, the five answers from your prompt, each saved as its own file. The idea is that a saved answer can be scored again and again.

In this course, your checker. check.py is the file on the Script track, and promptfooconfig.yaml is the file on the promptfoo track. The idea is that the same rules can be written as a script or as a config.

In this course, the folder in your project that holds your bad and polished-but-wrong outputs. The answer key is kept separately by the app and shown after the checker has run. The idea is a place for outputs whose right verdict you know.
In this course, the file that records your baseline as Iteration 0, ready for Part 4 to build on. The idea is a written record of each change and its score.
In this course, the chain of prompt, answer, file, checker and verdict. Every arrow is something you start, and nothing moves on by itself. The idea is that you can look at each link on its own.
In this course, what the checker says about one criterion on one saved answer: PASS, FAIL or NOT CHECKED. The idea is a result you can compare, not an opinion.
In this course, a new chat that sees only your prompt and notes, and writes the answers. The idea is to keep the writer of the answers apart from the rules that score them.
In this course, your AI tool working from your test cases. It writes the checker, the fixtures and the log. The idea is that the rules come from you and the code from a tool.
In this course, a folder that holds only your prompt, so the AI cannot see your test cases while it writes an answer. The idea is that answers must not bend to the rules that score them.
In this course, a model that is not the most powerful one your tool offers. You record its name because it goes in your log. The idea is that a score belongs to one prompt on one model.
The written description of what something must do. When a result is wrong, you change the spec first and let the checker follow.
In this course, one pass of the checker over a single saved answer, so you can see it work. It is not your baseline. The idea is that seeing a checker run is not yet a score you can trust.

In this course, the one of your five runs you pick as your best. Your checker should score it 95% or more. The idea is a check that a good answer is recognized as good. If it scores lower, look at the checker, not the prompt.
In this course, the AI tool you chose in setup, which runs in a terminal window inside this app. Its full name is command-line interface. The idea is that you use your own AI tool.
Plain text with a few simple symbols, such as # for a heading. Your prompt and your test cases are saved as .md files that any text editor can open.

A simple check that stands in for something a rule cannot judge directly, such as looking for a keyword instead of judging whether an answer is good. Tightening a proxy narrows the gap but never closes it.
An AI tool that does more than chat: it reads files, writes files and runs commands for you.
The words you give an AI tool to tell it what you need. The AI can only work from what the prompt says, so anything you leave out is a guess.
A checklist of labels, such as Role or Task, that names what a prompt needs, so you do not forget a part. Many exist, and you can build your own from the kinds of information your task needs.
Something you wanted in an answer that the prompt never said, so the AI had no way to know it.
A sample prompting framework with four labels: Role, Task, Context and Constraints. The letters use common expansions that other sources define differently.
A sample prompting framework with four labels: Role, Input, Steps and Expectation. The letters use common expansions that other sources define differently.

In this course, the prompt you write in your own words before you learn any structure, run once, so it shows your starting point. The idea is that you can only see what a structure adds by comparing it with where you began.
In this course, the short description of the Friday update, with the five things you know but that are not in the rough notes. The idea is that you score an answer against what was in your head.

A written description of one check an answer must pass: what to look for and the pass or fail rule for it. A file of test cases, saved with the input they apply to, is what a program can later use to score answers.
A criterion about how an answer looks, such as its length or its headings. It is right to check format when the task asks for a particular look.
A criterion about what an answer says, such as a fact it must contain. A set of criteria with only format checks can pass an answer that looks right and misses the point.

A list that a threshold points to, such as words to avoid or terms that must appear. You write it for your own task and keep it in the same file as the test cases, so the check can run from the file alone.
A question to ask of every threshold: could a script decide it with no human judgment? If not, tighten it into a number, a term or a label.

In this course, the table where you list your criteria, each with the requirement it traces to and its type, and later its threshold. The idea is that you draft all the rules in one place before you write them into a file.
